sheets.noticed: A quiet cream card with a small caption. The claim 'almost every solid sinks' is a hook I half caught.
A big 'ICE FLOATS.' title and an ice block sliding up. Something is happening now.
'Why does ice float?' over dots drifting in liquid water. The question keeps me.
Liquid water dots shift and settle under 'molecules tumble close'. Mild, but still moving.
The dots freeze into a grid and brown bonds snap into place. The lattice forming is satisfying to watch.
Hexagon bonds connect to four neighbours. Clear visual, I am still in.
The lattice opens into a wide hexagon pattern. Still evolving.
The hexagon is finished and mostly still, with a quiet gap. Lukewarm, but the payoff looks close.
'Ice takes more room' with liquid and ice side by side. Now I get the point.
Liquid dots against the open ice lattice. The comparison is easy to read.
'About 9% less dense' in bold orange. A concrete number lands.
'And it floats', then 'So it floats.' A clean ending on screen.
The closing card 'So it floats' stays up. I would stay to the end.

remembers: Water is unusual: when it freezes, its molecules lock into an open hexagonal lattice that takes up more room. So ice is about nine percent less dense than liquid water, and it floats.
